name: Click ID and query parameter stripping
plain: Browsers remove known tracking parameters from URLs before the site sees them, in some modes.
meaning: Controls whether a site can read the ad click ID at all. Safari strips in Private, Mail and Messages; Firefox in ETP Strict and Private; Brave in all modes by default; Chrome does not strip. Measurement teams lose attribution where stripping applies.

web.api: Browser feature (no site API); site sees URL without the parameter

access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

edge.note: Tracking prevention does not strip params

firefox.note: ETP Strict and Private only in release

limits.headline: Can remove known tracking codes from links before the site sees them, in some modes
limits.user_action: You open a link with a tracking code while using a browser privacy mode
can: Strip known tracking codes from a web address
Block the code from reaching the site
Work in Firefox and Safari in some privacy modes
cannot: Remove codes it does not know about
Run in Chrome, Edge or Samsung Internet by default
Hide a code if you share the link before it is cleaned
Stop trackers that use other methods like cookies or fingerprints
limits.differs: Firefox in strict or private mode and Safari in private browsing strip codes. Chrome and Edge do not.

story.what_it_is: Some browsers remove known tracking codes from web addresses before the site can read them.

marketing.name: Query parameter stripping
marketing.pitch: Firefox says it strips known tracking parameters in Strict mode and Private windows so sites cannot follow you by link.

marketing.name: Link Tracking Protection
marketing.pitch: Apple says Safari removes tracking parts of links in Private Browsing, Mail and Messages.

story.for_you: You click a link with a long tail of letters and nothing seems different. The browser quietly cuts off the tracking part, so the site never sees it. You may notice your ad gets less personal.
story.for_makers: Makers lose the click ID they use to prove an ad worked. They respond with server side tagging and other IDs. Browser makers use stripping to sell privacy, and ad teams must plan for it.

use_cases.example: A shopper uses Brave and clicks an ad. The click ID is stripped, so the sale cannot be tied to the ad.
A marketing team sees traffic from Safari as direct visits and cannot credit the right campaign.
A shared link with fbclid is cleaned in Messages, so the sender's tracking tail does not reach the friend.
A coupon site loses the code that proves a sale, and so gets less money from partners.
A game ad campaign cannot see which ads brought logged out players when the browser strips the click ID.
A phishing link often hides a tracking tail. Stripping it removes one way to tell which target clicked.

risks: Sites work around it with other IDs

technical_bounds: Works from a maintained list: unknown parameters pass through
Safari 27 beta adds Threads (xmt), YouTube (si) and X (twclid, cn, cxt) per a July 2026 code review; verify at release
Server side tagging with first-party capture before stripping can still record it only if the parameter reached the server

abuse: Not applicable; site side counter is dropping parameters into cookies earlier or using first-party redirects
